ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Surrender policy of Government for militants 
*41. SHRI S.S. AHLUWALIA: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the surrender policy of Government for members of militant/terrorist 
outfits who eschew violence and intend to return to the mainstream civil 
society; 
(b) whether it is uniform in ail the aff ected States or is at variance from 
one State to another; 
(c) whether distinctions, if any, are made between surrendering members 
belonging to outfits which have been operating at the behest of or linked to 
foreign espionage agencies and those who took to arms in pursuance of 
extremist ideological doctrines and /or fight against policies of Government 
perceived to be unjust; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS(SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATH): (a) 
to (e) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
The State of J&K, North Eastern States and major naxalite affected States 
have Surrender-cum-Rehabilitation Schemes for terrorists who want to shun 
violence and join the mainstream. Wh ile the Schemes in J&K and North 
Eastern States are identical, there are some variations in the Schemes 

RAJYA SABHA [27 July, 2005] 
being implemented in naxalite affected States. The benefits of these Schemes 
are, however, not available to foreign terrorists and espionage agents.

Threat of terrorist attacks 
*42. SHRI ANAND SHARMA: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the threat of terrorist attacks on 
national monuments and temple townships; and 
4 

[27 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) the steps proposed to meet the threat and protect places of national 
importance and religious worship? 
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATIL): (a) 
and (b) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. Intelligence inputs have been received regarding designs of 
terrorist groups to attack such places . These have also been shared with 
concerned States/UTs. 
(b) In view of the recent terroris t attack in Ayodhya, the security 
arrangements for places of national im portance like Taj Mahal at Agra and 
important places of religious worship at Ayodhya, Kashi and Mathura have 
been reviewed by the Union Government. Ministry of Home Affairs has 
also advised all the States/UTs to  immediately review the security 
arrangements for important religious  shrines, buildings of national 
importance, vital installations, high dignitaries and places of economic 
interest located within their jurisdiction, which may be most vulnerable to 
terrorist strikes and fidayeen attack. Further, they have also been requested 
to maintain extra vigil and sensitise their intelligence apparatus, for timely 
collection of threat inputs in this regard. Prompt sharing of intelligence 
and improved coordination, between all the security and intelligence 
agencies concerned,has also been emphasized to prevent any untoward 
incident in the future.. 
In addition, Government of India has been providing financial and 
material support to the States to modernize and strengthen their police forces. 
Central Para Military Forces have also been made available to the States for 
protection of such vulnerable places. 
SHRI ANAND SHARMA: Sir, I thank th e Home Minister for confirming 
through his statement the threat to national monuments from terrorists and 
also the possibility of fidayeen attacks. The statement does give a detailed 
account of the efforts being made to protect the monuments. We have seen 
recently the attack at Ayodhya, and be fore I ask the supplementary it is 
important to compliment the security forces for foiling the attack and killing 
all the militants. I would like to know fr om the hon. Minister that given this 
two-pronged strategy of the militants, that is, to

SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATIL: Sir, we receive lot of information and we 
disseminate that information to the State Governments, to the institutions and 
to the individuals also so that they can take the protective measures. 
Unfortunately, all that information, though it is with us, is not given wide

House into confidence and say that there is information that important 
national monuments, important scientific installations, important modern 
industries and some individuals who are respected in the country, individuals 
who are scientists, individuals who are in the modern industry, they have 
become vulnerable and we have given information to them also. 
Now, as far as the last part of your question is concerned, we have given 
this information to the State Government. We have asked them to look into 
the aspects relating to providing secu rity to the religious places, to the 
national monuments and to the individuals also, and, they have prepared the 
schemes. Those schemes have been discussed with Government of Indie also. 
Sir, the CISF is the force that is generally providing security to airports and 
other things also. Taj is also provided security by these people. These forces 
are there; they are being specially trai ned for these purposes. At some places, 
they are stationed. At Ayodhya, it was the para-military forces that were there

information. So, providing protection from outer circle, from the outer ring is 
generally left to them. But, this kind of special force is there. But, not one 
special force will be able to provide security to all the installations in all the 
States. We are doing it in cooperation with the State Governments.

stars, but reaching the mind of the man,  especially the mind of a terrorist is

Coordination in Poverty Alleviation Schemes 
*46. SHRI NAND KISHORE Y ADAV: Will the Minister of 
RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that for alleviating poverty in rural areas of the 
country it is necessary to remove unemployment; 
(b) if so, whether is is also a fact that many schemes are being run by 
Government at present for providing employment opportunities; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that people are not getting desired benefits of 
these schemes in the absence of mutual coordination among all the schemes; 
and 
(d) if so, the details of corrective steps Government propose to take for proper 
implementation of the said scheme? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (DR. RAGHUVANSH 
PRASAD SINGH): (a) to (d) Removal of unemployment is one of the necessary 
measures for the alleviation of poverty in the rural areas of the country. 
The Ministry of Rural Development is implementing two major 
employment generation Schemes namely Swarnyajanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana 
(SGSY) and Sampoorna Gramin Rozgar Yojana (SGRY) to provide self and 
wage employment to the families living below the poverty line in the rural areas of 
the country. The Government have also launched a new wage employment 
Scheme namely National Food For Works Programme (NFFWP) in 150 most 
backward districts of 27 States of the country to generate supplementary wage 
employment and providing food security through creation of need based 
economic, social and community assets in these districts.  The NFFWP will 
be open to the rural poor who are in need of wage employment-arid desire to do 
manual unskilled work. This programme will be replaced by the National 
Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme, the Bill for which has been introduced 
in the Parliament. 
In order to implement the schemes properly, the Ministry of Rural 
Development places special emphasis on monitoring and evaluation of its 
programmes being implemented through review by Union Ministers with Chief 
Ministers and other State Ministers concerned with the programmes of the 
Ministry, Performance Review Committee, Area Officer's Scheme,

Export of adulterated chillies 
*58.      SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: 
SHRIR.K.ANAND: 
Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have ascertained the facts regarding reported export of 
adulterated chillies, if so, the details thereof; 
(b) whether Government have taken up the issue on behalf of Indian exporters, if 
so, what steps are taken, if not, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether WTO agreements provide for sanitary-standards, if so, are they 
standardised, if so, the details thereof, if not. the reasons therefor; and 
(d) whether Government have also ascertained that the 
sanitary-standards are not used as non-tariff barriers against agro-exports 
from developing countries, if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI KAMAL 
NATH): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The reports regarding export of adulterated chillies refer 
mostly to the presence of the prohibited Sudan I to IV dyes in chilli exported to 
European Union (EU). Since 2003, European Commission has issued about 61 
rapid alerts claiming presence of Sudan dyes in chillies/chilli products exported 
from India or in food products exported from India or in food products manufactured 
in the EU using chilli powder/chilli products in sourced from India. However, in 
February-March, 2005, Food Standard Agency (FSA), United Kingdom, 
ordered recall of food stuffs contaminated with Sudan dyes. The chilli powder 
claimed to have been used in the manufacture of recalled products in UK was 
exported in 2002, before the introduction 
40 

[27 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
of the mandatory testing regime of the Spices Board for chilli powder/ chilli 
products. 
Government has expressed its concern to the EU authorities over the manner and the 
procedure governing the issuance of rapid alerts. 
(c) The Sanitary and Phytosanitary (SPS) Agreement of WTO provides for 
notification of sanitary standards prior to their enforcement in order to provide trading 
partners an opportunity to comment thereon and these comments have to be taken into 
account before finalizing and enforcing the standards/measures. 
(d) Sanitary and phytosanitary standards are not to be used as non-iariff barriers. 
Under the SPS agreement, WTO member countries are permitted to impose only 
those requirements/measures, which are based on scientific principles and are needed to 
protect public health. The Government can challenge another country's food safety or 
plant health requirements can challenge another country's food safety or plant health 
requirements on the ground that they are not justified by scientific evidence. The 
transparency in the SPS measures discourages countries to use them as non-tariff 
barriers.

Sanitary and phytosanitary standards for agro and farm products 
243. SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: 
SHRIR.K.ANAND:  
        SHRI KB. KRISHNAMURTHY:  
         SHRI HARISH RAWAT: 
Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the WTO agreement provide for Sanitary and Phytosanitary 
standards for agro and farm products; 
(b) if so, what is the mechanism to prescribe such standards; 
(c) what are the guarantees to avoid such standards from being used as non-
tariff barriers; and 
(d) what steps are being taken to enhance Sanitary and Phytosanitary 
Standards of the country's exports? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) Yes, Sir. The Agreement on 
the Application of Sanitary and Phytosanitary measures provides for Sanitary 
and Phytosanitary standards for agro and farm products. 
(b) The mechanism for providing such standard is through notifying the new 
or any amendment in the existing stan dards to the WTO, in case, these 
standards are different from the international standards as set by the 
International Plant Protection Convention (IPCC) or such standards would 
have significant trade effect. 
(c) The SPS Agreement in WTO provides that the Sanitary and 
Phytosanitary standards are not to be used as non-tariff barriers. In case, the 
exporter feels that any WTO Member is  using these as non-tariff barrier, the 
Government has the right to ask for the scientific evidences which led to 
imposition of such Sanitary and Phytosanitay measures. The SPS agreement 
has been provided with clear and detailed rights and obligations for food safety and 
plant health measures which affect trad e. Countries are permitted to impose 
only those requirements which are needed to protect health, and these 
requirements have to be based on scientific principle. The Government can 
challenge another country's food safety or plant health requirements on the 
ground that they are not justified by 
58 

[27 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
scientific evidence. The procedures and decisions used by the country in 
assessing the risks to food safety or plant and animal health has to be made 
available to other countries on request. This brings in the transparency in the SPS 
Measures which discourages countries to use SPS measures as non-tariff 
barriers. 
(d) In order to enhance sanitary and phytosanitary standards of the 
country's exports, following major steps have been taken: 
(i) Certification agencies have been established; 
(ii) Export Inspection Councils have been strengthened; 
(iii) Capacity building exercise of the exporters through trainings, 
seminars, etc. have been undertaken; 
(iv) Duty free import of equipments such as panels etc. for meeting the SPS 
Standards have been allowed; 
(v) Residue monitoring plans for specified commodities are being carried out; 
(vi) compulsory testing regimes have been put in place for certain 
specified commodities before consignment are exported out; and 
(vii) exporters are being given financial assistance for quality testing of certain 
specified exportable produces.

Percentage of people living below the poverty line 
307. SHRI T.T.V. DHINAKARAN: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the year in which the latest study was done to ascertain the percentage of 
people living below the poverty line State-wise; 
(b) the details of such survey; 
(c) the criteria on which the poverty is assessed; 
(d) the concessions provided to the people living below the poverty line; and 
(e) time frame by which poverty shall be completely eradicated? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SURYAKANTA PATIL): (a) and (b) The 
Planning Commission estimates the incidence of poverty at national and State level from 
the large sample survey on household consumer expenditure conducted by the National 
Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO) at an interval of approximately five years. The 
latest quinquennial round of survey, on the basis of which data on the percentage of people 
living below the poverty line was ascertained, was done in the year 1999-2000 (55th 
Round). The State-wise information on percentage of people living below the poverty line 
during 1999-2000 is given in the enclosed Statement (See below). 
(c) The Planning Commission uses the per capita consumption expenditure as 
the criteria to determine the persons living below poverty 
116

line. According to the latest large sample survey conducted by NSSO during 
1999-2000 (NSS 55th round), people who could not spend the prescribed per 
capita consumption expenditure of Rs. 327.56. per month in rural areas and Rs. 
454.11 per capita per month in urban areas were considered as poor. 
(d) and (e) The Ministry of Rural Development implements a self 
employment programme viz., Swarajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) 
under which the Swarozgaries from the BPL families are provided credit and 
subsidy to acquire economic assets for their sustainable employment. Under 
Sampoorna Grameen Rozgar Yojana (SGRY) and National Food for Work

families for construction of houses.    
The Tenth Five Year Plan (2002-07) has set a target for reduction of poverty

Sanitation facilities in rural India 
311. SHRIMATI SUKHBUNS KAUR:  Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the number and percentage of population in rural India, particularly the 
Northern States who have still no access to sanitation facilities even 58 years 
after Independence; and 
(b) the progress made In providing such facilities during the Ninth and Tenth 
Five Year Plans so far; and the expenditure incurred thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI A. NARENDRA): (a) As per Census 2001,10.80 
crore rural households representing 78.11% of total number of rural 
households in the country, did not have access to sanitation facilities. The 
information related to Northern States is given in the enclosed Statement (See 
below). 
(b) To accelerate pace of rural sanitati on coverage in India, a centrally 
sponsored programme, namely Central Rural Sanitation Programme (CRSP), was 
introduced in 1986, and restructured as Total Sanitation Campaign in the year 
1999.51.12 lakh household toilets were constructed under CRSP during the Ninth 
Plan with total expenditure of Rs. 892.76 crore. Under TSC, 1.43 crore household 
toilets have been constructed during the Ninth and Tenth Plans so far. In addition, 
under the TSC, 1.5 lakhs school toilets, 0.25 lakhs Anganwadi toilets and 4,933 
community complexes were also constructed during this period. Rs 1221.47 crore 
has been spent on sanitation promotion under TSC during the Ninth and Tenth 
Plans.

Development of KBK districts of Orissa 
312. SHRI SURENDRA LATH: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the total amount allocated till 31 st March, 2005 under the long-term action 
plan formulated and implemented for all round development of Kalahandi, 
Boiangir and Koraput (KBK) districts of Orissa; 
(b) the economic, educational and social upliftment in overall living 
standard of residents of the said districts due to allocation of the said amount; 
(c) whether it is a fact that there has not been any expected improvement in the 
overall living standard of natives of the said districts in comparison to the 
amount allocated by Government; and 
(d) if so, the reasons therefor and the action being taken by Government for 
improving their living standards? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SURYAKANTA PATIL): (a) Total amount of 
Rs. 4287.65 crores, including Additional Central Assistance/Special Central 
Assistance of Rs. 943.95 crore, flowed to the KBK districts from 1998-99 to 
2004-05. 
. (b) The following major achievements have been made in different sectors of the 
KBK districts to raise the economic, educational, social and overall living 
standards of the people of the KBK region. 
* 2 lakh old, infirm and indigent persons are being covered annually under 
Emergency Feeding Programme. 
* 9.42 lakh children under the age group 0-6 and other beneficiaries have 
been covered under Special Nutrition Programme annually.

districts providing treatment to nearly 13 lakh patients annually at their 
doorsteps.

(d) Government has been taking a number of steps from time to time to

staple fibres, the whole value addition chain has been given excise 
exemption option.

been allowed at concessional rate  of customs duty to encourage 
investments and to make our textile products competetive in the 
global market. The cost of machinery has also been reduced through 
fiscal policy measures.

Decline in textile exports 
† 333. SHRI MOTILAL VORA: 
SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA: 
Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased to state: 
(a) the decline in the export of textiles from India and percentage increase in the export of 
textiles from China after the end of 'quota raj' since January 2005; 
(b) the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the steps being taken by Government to ensure that textile export industry could 
sustain itself in the competitive market and by when results thereof are likely to be 
achieved? 
THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI SHANKERSINH VAGHELA): (a) 
According to the provisions DGCI&S data for January-March 2005, the exports of 
textiles and clothing (including handicrafts, jute and coir) had  
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
161 

RAJYA SABHA [27 JULY, 2005] 
amounted to Rs. 14,857 crores during the period January-March, 2005 as compared to 
the exports of Rs. 19,178 crores during the corresponding period of 2004, showing a 
decline of 22.5%. However, as per the latest available DGCI&S provisional data, 
there has been a positive growth of 13.7% in textile exports during the month of Apirl, 
2005 compared to April, 2004. 
European Union (EU) and United States (US) account for more than 60% of 
India's textile exports. The trade data of EU/US authorities show increased textile 
imports from India and China in the post quota period. According to the US Trade Data, 
the US textiles and clothing imports from China have increased by 60.02% and from 
India by 29.49% during the period January-May, 2005 in comparison to the 
corresponding period of previous year. According to EU Trade Data, China has recorded 
a growth of 46.3% and India 12.2% in the EU-15 imports of textiles and clothing 
Kerns, during the period January-March, 2005 in comparison to the corresponding 
period of previous year; 
(b) The main reasons attributed to the decline in textile exports during January-
March '05 are as follows: 
(i) There has been a downward pressure on prices, consequent upon dismantling of 
quota regime. 
(J) China has been able to withstand the downward pressure on prices as it has large 
production capacities with economies of scale. 
(Hi) The reduction in DEPB rates in September, 2004 had the effect of squeezing 
margins of Indian exporters. The fall in exports has been more pronounced 
in cotton textiles where the cut in DEPB rates were the deepest. 
(C) Government has been taking a number of steps from time to time to strengthen 
Indian textile industry for meeting the growing global competition. Some of the important 
initiatives taken are: • 
(i) The Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS) has been made operational 
from 1-4-1999 to facilitate the modernisation and upgradation of the 
sector. 
(I) To improve the productivity and quality of cotton, Government has launched 
Technology Mission on Cotton (TMC). The mission 
162 

[27 JULY, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
comprises four mini-missions, which are being jointly implemented by the 
Ministry of Agriculture and Ministry of Textiles. One of the important 
ingredients of the Mission is to improve cotton processing facilities by 
upgrading/modernizing the existing ginning and pressing facilities and setting 
up of new market yards/improvement of existing market yards. 
(iii) The Government has launched a Centrally Sponsored Scheme titled 
"Apparel Park for Export Scheme" for imparting focused thrust for setting up 
of apparel manufacturing units of international standards at potential growth 
centres to give fillip to exports. 
(IV) For upgrading infrastructure facilities at important textile centres, a scheme titled 
Textile Centre Infrastructure Development Scheme" (TCIDS) has been 
launched. 
(v) The fiscal duty structure has been generally rationalised to achieve growth and 
maximum value addition within the country. Except for mandatory excise 
duty on man-made filament yams and man-made staple fibres, the whole value 
addition chain has been given excise exemption option. 
(vi) The imports of specified textiles and garment machinery items has been 
allowed at concessional rate of customs duty to encourage investments 
and to make our textile products competitive in the global market. The cost 
of machinery has also been reduced through fiscal policy measures. 
(vii) Duty-free imports of 21 items of trimmings and embellishment items are 
allowed to the garment exporters, upto 3% of their actual export performance 
during the previous year. 
(viii) National Institute for Fashion Technology (NIFT), its seven branches and apparel 
Training & Design Centres (ATDCs) are running various courses/programmes to 
meet skilled manpower requirements of textile industry especially apparel 
in the field of design, merchandising and marketing. 
(ix) Facilities by way of eco-testing laboratories have been created to enable 
exporters to get the garments/textiles pre-tested for conforming to the 
requirements of importing countries. 
163 

RAJYA SABHA [ 27 JULY, 2005] 
(x) 100% Foreign Direct Investment is allowed in the textile sector under 
the automatic route. 
(xi) The Government has de-reserved the readymade garments, hosiery and 
knitwear from the SSI sector. 
The above initiatives have helped the textile export industry in sustaining itself in 
the global market.

Re: Grave situation prevailing in Gurgaon due to agitation by workers 
of Honda motor cycles and scooters India 
SHRI NILOTPAL BASU (West Bengal): Mr. Chairman, Sir. with your 
permission I would like to draw the attention of the House to the very, very grave 
situation which has come to prevail in Gurgaon, Haryana, as a result of the agitation 
by the workers, and the attitude of the management of the Honda Company. I 
think it is necessary to put the whole issue in proper perspective. I visited the 
place, and, particularly, the General Hospital, 
168 

[27 JULY, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Gurgaon, yesterday along with the Member - elect of this House, Mrs. 
Brinda Karat. 
Sir, the situation prevailing there is very, very unfortunate. After what 
happened day-before-yesterday, which all of us have seen over the television; 
the electronic media, the situation c ontinued to remain very critical in 
Gurgaon yesterday as well. In fact, in front of our eyes, there was a second 
round of lathicharge and firing of teargas shells within the hospital premises 
itself. 
Now, sir, I will come to the issue which sparked off a sequence of this 
very unfortunate development. It arises out of the flagrant violation of labour 
laws enacted by this august House along with the other august House. 
There are several provisions in our laws about trade unions rights, and as 
per international covenant of the ILO also, those laws have to be respected 
in the country because certain questions are also coming up now in the 
context of what happened day-before-yesterday, and yesterday that whether 
this will, actually, have a negative e ffect or an adverse effect on the 
investment climate of the country. I think we have to understand that 
whosoever is, actually, investing and running a facility in this country will 
have to abide by the laws of this country as much as they abide by the 
laws of their home countries wherever they continue to carry on economic 
activities. 
Now, Sir, a lot of things are being said, but this entire chain of events 
started in December last,—the present Government in Haryana had not 
come in place—from the earlier Government itself, in December 2004, 
when one of the Managers of the Honda Company blatantly kicked a 
worker. If you look at the situation in the Honda Company, there are about 
1600 workers who are on the permanent roles and 1400 are temporary 
workers, and there are stiff conditions for the conferment of the jobs of 
these workers. In spite of the persistent efforts of the workers to register a 
trade union, that could not take place earlier. Now , these things have 
been happening, and there is a grave at mosphere of uncertainty there 
among the workers, and it led to the protest demonstration day-before-
yesterday and led to an altercation with the police. Now, I know—the hon. 
Home Minister is sitting here—that for the Government of India to intervene 
directly, that is not possible. But, I think it is possible for the Government 
of India to send advisories to the State Government. Sir, the situation that 
169 

RAJYA SABHA [27 JULY, 2005] 
is prevailing there is actually an expression of a total collapse of the credibility 
of the local Administration. In fact, yesterday's incident— if you look at— took 
place, was triggered off by the presence of the Deputy Commissioner there 
who is widely believed to have spearheaded the barbaric attack on the 
workers day-before-yesterday, and the Superintendent of Police, 
Gurgaon also played a very, very destructive role in handling the situation day-
before-yesterday. Sir, we are aware of the Government's decision to have a 
judicial inquiry ordered in this case. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Everything will be covered under the judicial inquiry.

SHRI SHANKAR ROY CHOWDHURY  (West Bengal): Mr. Vice-
Chairman, Sir, to begin with, I would like to complement the Ministry of Home 
Affairs, which means the Home Minister. I would like to compliment the Ministry of 
Home Affairs of the previous Government also because this is an on-going 
struggle, an on-going combat and every Home Ministry and every Government 
has been doing its best. We are fortunate to have, notwithstanding the 
incidents we see on the television, extremely competent agencies both in our 
police, in our internal security organisations and in our intelligence. The subject of 
today's discussion is cross border terrorism 
226 

[27 JULY, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
and terrorist acts. I do not know whether the choice of word has been by design 
or by accident, but these are indeed two separate things. Cross border 
terrorism means people who come across the border, and terrorist acts mean 
people who are already in situ. I think the attack on Ayodhya is a good example 
of what is the subject of this discussion. So far as the attack on Ayodhya is 
concerned, the preparation for the attack started off in Mendhar in Jammu and 
Kashmir. Arms were brought across put in a specially constructed Tata Sumo 
brought all the way from Mendhar to Panipat. The people who carried out the 
attack came from Nepal. They stayed in a safe house; married up with the 
arms and ammunition and then they carried out this attack. That means, 
people came from across the border and there were people inside the border 
who could support them. The fight is against the both. What is this situation? 
Cross border terrorism is coming from the west, that is, the border with 
Pakistan. The Pakistan border, regardless of what we may say, is 
reasonably well defended. We have got a fence. Everything is in position. I 
think the terrorists from Pakistan who are coming across, notwithstanding the 
incident of Ayodhya, are finding it more and more difficult to get across. Of course, 
the fencing along the LoC has been damaged due to the recent snowfall. I 
hope it will be made ready in time. But our gaps are in the east and on the 
Nepal border. The eastern border is wide open. The Border Security Force, 
as all of you know, is meant to defend or watch a distance of about 30 to 40 
kilometers which is the distance they watch in the western sector. In the 
eastern sector in West Bengal, Tripura and Assam a single BSF Battalion is 
covering nearly 70 to 90 kilometers. In Tripura, they are covering 90 
kilometres. I think, there were decision taken that they will move the BSF fact 
to the eastern sector, but that has not taken place yet. Sir, I would, through you, 
urge the Government and the Minister to give a thought to the eastern sector 
because the eastern sector is a backdoor which is more or less wide 
open. 
The second is the border with Nepal. It is supposed to be an unfenced 
border which is not manned because of the special relationship we have with 
Nepal. But now we have felt the necessity to keep a border guarding force on 
the Nepal border also. We have given it to the SSB. Now with due respect to the 
Government and to the Force, this is not a very high grade Force as yet. If you 
insist on making the SSB guard the border, please see to it that the SSB 
comes up to the standards of the BSF as soon as 
227 

RAJYA SABHA [27 JULY, 2005] 
possible because this is a wide open border through which all these 
incidents are taking place. 
Really speaking, there are three types of terrorisms in India, that is, Jehadi 
terrorism, Naxalite terrorism and North Eastern terrorism based on ethnic groups. 
To my mind, the biggest threat that is confronting India today is the Naxalite 
terrorism which is holding the entire centre of India, In this, the biggest weapon is 
good governance and police reform. This is the most dangerous form of terrorism 
which is threatening our country and I do think that the Centre's decision that the 
States will combat Naxalite terrorism on their own is a mistaken decision so 
far. I do think that there has to be a coordinated activity between the States. In 
the North East, in Jammu and Kashmir, the lead agency de factor became the 
Army. That is spread across the inter-State borders. So operations could be 
continuously carried out. But when you are using a police force to contain a 
particular type of terrorism and you say that it has to be by the States, I think this 
is not the right method of tackling the Naxalite terrorism. There has to be a 
certain methodology worked out in the North East. There was a lot of talk that the 
North Eastern Council should be made responsible at one point of time. But it did 
not work due to various reasons. The Centre has got to explore ways and 
means whereby the Naxalite-infested States, namely, the seven in number, 
could form some sort of a common grid. The Centre must impress upon the 
States to create a similar organisation that is there in the North-East and in 
Jammu and Kashmir, that is, a unified headquarter. Here, of course, there 
will be various elements in it. But, until these States seriously set up 
organisations like unified headquarters, it will not work. It has been 
mentioned, time and again, that good governance is the key to tackling the 
Naxalite activity. All the areas where the Naxalite activities take place are the 
tribal areas. They are the most under-developed areas in underdeveloped States. 
Now, how do we go about it? We have a federal structure whereby everything 
has to go through the States and, I think, the Prime Minister himself is worried 
about it because the vast amount of resources are going into good 
governance, but the delivery system at the grassroots level remains the 
same. So, my suggestion, as always been, is please create Special 
Development Zones. And, whether the system of governance will be through the 
States, through the Centre, or the amalgamation of both, these have to be 
worked out, because unless you get good governance, you will not be able to fight 
the 
228 

[27 JULY, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Naxalite menace. 
As far as police reforms are concerned, it is, of course easy to say that one 
must tackle the root-cause of Naxafism or, any other form of terrorism, for that 
matter. But the projection of the Government in most of these cases is the 
police force, and the police force has to be reformed not only at the top level, 
but.critically, it must be reformed at the lowest level, that is at the level of the 
Thana. Today, your police, force is discredited because it is not functioning at the 
level where it comes in contact with the people, and that is, not at the level of the 
States headquarters, but it is at the level of the Thana. Unless you get good, well-
trained police force, well-equipped, well-motivated one, working at the Thana 
level, I am afraid that this is not going to work. A mention was made that 
warnings are conveyed to States. I would just like to say that it is very difficult to 
convey warnings with any specifics. It cannot say that there will be an attack on 
Ayodhya on such and such date and at such and such time; it has to be a 
general term. And, under those warnings, every religious institution and, 
particularly, the temples, are under threat in this country at any time. 
In conclusion, let me say that our people are eminently sensisble. In spite 
of the various problems that we have got, the aim of these attacks on temples are 
obviously to weaken the communal harmony. But I think, our people have got 
enough common sense, enough goodwill. So, in spite of what we say, from 
time to time, notwithstanding instances which have taken place earlier, I don't 
think we are going to see any major communal outbreak in this country 
because, as you say, whether in Jammu and Kashmir or in the North-East, 
people of India also want peace. Thank you.

giving them Rs. 2,000 or so a month. I am sometimes told that Rs. 20—30 is 
given to them, and they are w illing to go. Now, they are not ideologically 
motivated, and they are not fundamentalist as well. They also do not have any 
political acts to commit. Yet, because of the sheer force of circumstances, they 
are taking

RAJYA SABHA [27 JULY, 2005]  
to terrorism. It is our responsibility to see that employment is generated, and that 
is the Government of India's policy in creating the Employment Guarantee 
Scheme. The Employment Guarantee Scheme will be criticised left and right by 
some people. There will be difficulties in it, and there will be some mistakes 
committed also. Yet, where the Employment Guarantee Scheme or schemes of 
the nature have been in existence, the terrorist activities are at their lowest 
ebb. This is also to be understood. Then, there is fundamentalism. Now, religion 
instead of uniting people, it is dividing us. i am not blaming any one religion for that 
matter, or, anybody who is adopting that kind of religion. Then, there is some 
kind of intellectual philosophy, the class of civilisation and thing like that. They are 
responsible for it. And, I agree with Shri Shankar Roy Chowdhury that one of 
the antidotes is good governance. If good governance is provided at the 
grassroots level, at the taluka level, at the district level, at the State level and at 
the Union level, the possibilities of terrorist activities will be reduced. But, at the 
national level, we are in the process of planning. At the State level, we are in the 
process of planning and implementation. At the district level and at the lower level, 
We are actually not in the process of planning. A little bit of planning is also required 
and implementation of it. And that is the cutting edge of administration. If at that 
cutting edge of administration, good governance is not good, then,it becomes 
difficult. That is why Shri Rajiv Gandhi created the Panchayati Raj system. And 
that system has to be used in such a fashion as to ensure that there is good 
governance at that level, that in the matter distribution of land, distribution of 
house-sites, distribution of foodgrains, distribution of kerosene, distribution of 
subsidies given to them, it has to be done in such a fashion that they don't feel that 
injustive has been done to them. Supposing the Government of India wants to 
give a house-site under the Indira Awaas Yojana, and the house-site is given to 
a person who is related to one of the politicians, then, others feel unhappy. If it is 
given to one of the relatives of a Government servant, others feel unhappy. If he is 
deserving, then, nobody will feel unhappy. But if he is not deserving and it is given 
on that account, then,they feel unhappy. So, good governance is also necessary. 
And, then, it is also necessary to see that harmony is maintained. What is being 
done? Now, in fact, this forum is there here, we come and we discuss many 
important issues, issues which are of international importance, issues which are 
of national importance, issues which are going to have an impact on the minds, 
hearts and lives of the people in the country, in the neighbouring 
262 

[27 JULY, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
country and also in the world. Here, what is it that we are doing? Are we 
really trying to understand the problems, trying to suggest solution or are 
we only inclined to criticise one or the other? Now, if the present 
Government is there, the past Government is criticised. Or, the Opposition 
criticises the present Government. Now, if this kind of a thing is done, it is 
not going to help. If the terrorist activites are taking place,— I am sorry to 
say; I am sometimes very unhappy to hear what is said on the floor of the 
House— it is not the terrorists who are criticised. But it is the members of 
the forces who are criticised. Now the people sitting here—please don't 
feel that I am trying to offend anybody—criticised the police like anything. 
But then, when I was sitting here, I felt that six policemen died for saving 
the lives of the people in Parliame nt. If they had not been there, the 
history of India would have been different. We forget that and we criticised 
not the terrorists; but we criticis e the policemen. Policemen should be 
criticised. Policemen should be punished, if it is necessary, if they have 
committed mistakes, and we will not commit any error in doing that. But 
to blacken them or cover them with black colour and saying that all of 
them are like that is not proper. I know so many people who are dying for 
the people who are unconnected to them. A man from Kerala dying in 
Nagaland! I have seen them. They do not have their relatives living there 
and yet, they are facing bullets there. They are losing their limbs there. 
And some of them have lost their lives we do not remember them. They 
too have their fundamental rights. They too have their human rights. They 
too have their sacrifices in their lives. If we forget their sacrifices, it is going 
to be very, very difficult. So, on the one hand, while criticising, let us not go 
to the other extreme. I am not saying that they should not be criticised. I 
am not saying that the Home Minister should not be criticised. When you 
criticise, you suggest certain things to us. And if I am wise enough, I will 
accept your suggestion. If I am not wise enough, I will just pay you back in 
the same coin and make you keep quiet; I can do that. But I am not doing 
that. You should criticise, but, at the same time, you also understand the 
difficulties. What is the populaion of the country? What is the number of 
policemen who are taking care of all these things? what are the kind of 
duties that they have to do? They have to do the duties of protecting the 
borders. They have to see that no terrorist activity takes place here. They 
have to do all sorts of things. And when everybody is agitated, they have to 
be there. Sometimes they behave; sometimes they misbehave also. They 
should not, and whenever they misbehave they can rest assured that action

would criticise the police or the officers, but we will not criticise those people who

deflecting the attention from the real culprits to the culprits who are not equally

As far as Ayodhya is concerened statements were made by the hon.

as the people inside were concerened it was a very strong structure; they could 
not enter. Otherwise they could have created problems. But so far as things 
outside were concerned, we did have discussions with the State Government 
and the State Government also agreed that if certain things had to be done, it 
would do them. So we are not doing them in an ad hoc manner. We have 
appointed a committee of experts and the people who are in the business of 
providing protection to these kinds of structures would make the suggestions 
and we will strengthen them. I can assure this House that we are taking 
steps to protect all other places also places of historic importance pieces of 
religious importance and leaders also. But you will understand how many religious 
places are there how many important histrocial places are there and how many 
important individulas or VIPs are there arid at how many places the police can 
be there or protection can be there. We will leave no stone unturned to 
provide the best of protection to all the installations and to these personalities. 
Yet we will keep praying that nothing happpens. Now that is what we will do. If 
something good happens the credit should go to those people who are actually 
there in the field, in spite of the fact that some political statements were made 
fey some persons, I do not think that those political statements were as 
important as the good suggestions made by them. And the hon. Members can 
rest assured that all the good suggestions made by them will be borne in mind by 
us and we will,certainly like to act upon them and we would like to do our best.

SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH: Sir, I would like to hon. Home Minister to clarify 
whether he said that at the end of the two-years time everybody living in the 
North-East will have a multipurpose identity card. 
SHRI SHIVRAJ V.PATIL: Sir, the border between Nepal and India cannot be 
fenced The peole wanting to go to the Nepal don't need any paper from the Nepal 
Government and the Indian Government and the people wanting to come to India 
don't need any paper. That is the kind of agreement we have with that country. 
But it is a fact that the Naxalite Movement has developed on both sides 
probably more in Nepal than in India and that is causing some concern to us. It is 
a fact that as the hon. Member said in the field post something happened which 
had not happened in the past. We have taken note of it and we are going to 
strengthen our forces over there. Today that border is not protected by the 
Border Security Force. It is protected by the SSB. That is a new force and 
exactly, Mr. Shankar Roy Chowdhury knows it. That is a force which was created 
for performing a different kind of duty. But that duty is not being performed by that 
force. He also suggested that let that force be better trained let the strength of 
that force by increased and let that job be done in a proper manner. We have 
accepted this thing and we would like to strengthen the force that is over there. We 
would like to give them better equipment, better information and try to see to it that 
the incidents of the nature which happened in Lakhimpur do not occur. We will 
strengthen the State police also. These are some of the things. 
Border protection is done by the Government of India. There is no doubt about it. 
But the internal protection or security duty is done by the State police. We 
would like to strengthen the State police also. About that queston, I do not 
think it is necessary for me to answer in detail. 
About Mr. Jairam Ramesh's question we are very seriously thinking of giving 
multi-purpose identity cards to all. This project has been considered by us and it 
requires a lot of money. New concepts are given to us. Some people say," Give 
them cards which help them to vote," Make multi-purpose cards, this and that. And 
they are saying that a lot of money would be required and all those things. 
266 

[27 JULY, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
We have decided to provide multi-purpose identity cards to the people in 
the bordering areas in the border States. A pilot project has been accepted. 
We are in the process of selecting a design for the card and the information 
which was required to be collected first, so as to prepare cards has 
also been prepared. The pilot project is there. I think it will be possible 
for the Government of India to provide the cards within a two year time in the 
bordering areas where the pilot project is there. Please do not take it as an 
assurance and I am saying that we are at it and, we would do it.
